items.prompt: What are the three main sections of an insect's body called?

options.label: Head, thorax, and abdomen
options.feedback: Correct. The insect body is divided into these three parts, each with its own set of jobs.

options.label: Head, chest, and belly
options.feedback: Those are everyday names, but the scientific terms are head, thorax, and abdomen.

options.label: Skull, trunk, and tail
options.feedback: Those words describe a vertebrate body, not an insect. An insect has three distinct sections, not a skull and tail.

options.label: Front, middle, and back
options.feedback: That describes positions, not the actual body sections. The sections are named head, thorax, and abdomen.

items.ok_line: Insects have a head, thorax, and abdomen.
items.exp_text: All insects share a body made of three sections: the head, the thorax, and the abdomen. The head holds the eyes, antennae, and mouthparts; the thorax carries the legs and wings; the abdomen contains most of the internal organs.

items.prompt: What covers the outside of an insect's body?

options.label: A soft skin like a worm's
options.feedback: Insects do not have soft skin. A hard outer covering called an exoskeleton gives them support and protection.

options.label: A shell made of bone
options.feedback: Insects have no bones at all. Their outer covering is called an exoskeleton and it is not made of bone.

options.label: A hard outer skeleton called an exoskeleton
options.feedback: Correct. This outer skeleton supports the body, protects it, and gives muscles something to pull against.

options.label: A layer of mucus and scales
options.feedback: That is not how an insect's body is covered. Mucus and scales belong to other animals, not insects.

items.ko_line: Insects have a hard exoskeleton, not skin or bone.
items.exp_text: An insect is covered by a tough outer layer called an exoskeleton. This skeleton is on the outside, not inside like our bones, and it gives the body its shape and strength.

items.prompt: How many antennae does an insect have?

options.label: One
options.feedback: Insects never have only one antenna. They always come in pairs, one on each side of the head.

options.label: Two
options.feedback: Correct. Insects have exactly two antennae, which they use for sensing smell, touch, and vibrations.

options.label: Four
options.feedback: Four antennae would be two pairs, but insects have only one pair. Spiders, not insects, sometimes have more legs but still two antennae.

options.label: None
options.feedback: All insects have antennae. Some may be very short or hidden, but they are always there.

items.ko_line: Insects always have exactly two antennae.
items.exp_text: Every insect has two antennae, one on each side of its head. They are sense organs that help the insect feel its surroundings and detect chemicals in the air.

items.prompt: How many legs does an insect have in total?

options.label: Four
options.feedback: Four legs is the number for many vertebrates like dogs and cats. Insects have three pairs, which makes six legs.

options.label: Eight
options.feedback: Eight legs is the number for spiders and other arachnids, not insects. Insects have six legs.

options.label: Ten
options.feedback: Ten legs is far too many for an insect. Arthropods like crabs may have ten, but insects are built with exactly six.

options.label: Six
options.feedback: Correct. All insects have six legs, arranged as three pairs attached to the thorax.

items.ok_line: Insects have six legs in three pairs.
items.ko_line: Insects have six legs, not four, eight, or ten.
items.exp_text: An insect always has six legs. They are attached to the thorax in three pairs, and this is one of the key features that distinguishes an insect from a spider, which has eight.

items.prompt: Which part of an insect's body carries the eyes and mouthparts?

options.label: The head
options.feedback: Correct. The head is the front section and holds the sensory organs and the mouth.

options.label: The thorax
options.feedback: The thorax carries the legs and wings, not the eyes or mouth. Those are on the head.

options.label: The abdomen
options.feedback: The abdomen holds organs like the stomach and reproductive system, not the eyes or mouth.

options.label: The tail
options.feedback: Insects do not have a tail section. The body ends with the abdomen, not a tail.

items.ok_line: The head holds eyes and mouthparts.
items.ko_line: Eyes and mouth are on the head, not thorax or abdomen.
items.exp_text: The head is the front section of an insect. It carries the eyes, the antennae, and the mouthparts, so it is the part that sees, senses, and takes in food.

items.prompt: What is the correct order of an insect's body sections from front to back?

options.label: Abdomen, head, thorax
options.feedback: That order is backward. The head is at the front, then thorax, then abdomen.

options.label: Thorax, abdomen, head
options.feedback: The head comes first, not the thorax. The correct order is head, thorax, abdomen.

options.label: Head, thorax, abdomen
options.feedback: Correct. From front to back, an insect has its head, then its thorax, then its abdomen.

options.label: Head, abdomen, thorax
options.feedback: The thorax comes before the abdomen, not after it. The middle section is the thorax.

items.ok_line: Front to back: head, thorax, abdomen.
items.ko_line: The thorax sits between the head and the abdomen.
items.exp_text: When you look at an insect from the front, you first see the head, then the thorax in the middle, and finally the abdomen at the rear. This order is the same for every insect.

items.prompt: What do the small holes on the sides of an insect's body do?

options.label: They let the insect see
options.feedback: Those holes are spiracles, not eyes. The eyes are on the head, made of many tiny lenses.

options.label: They release liquid waste
options.feedback: Insects do not use those holes for waste. The spiracles are for breathing.

options.label: They produce sound
options.feedback: Sound is made by legs or wings rubbing, not by these holes. The holes are breathing openings.

options.label: They let air enter the body
options.feedback: Correct. These holes, called spiracles, open into a network of tubes that carry air directly to the insect's tissues.

items.ok_line: Spiracles let air into the body.
items.ko_line: The side holes are spiracles, used for breathing.
items.exp_text: Insects breathe through small openings called spiracles along the sides of their abdomen and thorax. Air enters these holes and travels through tiny tubes to reach every part of the body without needing lungs.

items.prompt: What is the main part of an insect's body that contains its stomach and intestines?

options.label: The head
options.feedback: The head contains the brain and mouthparts, not the stomach. Digestion happens further back.

options.label: The abdomen
options.feedback: Correct. The abdomen is the rear section and houses the digestive organs, heart, and reproductive parts.

options.label: The thorax
options.feedback: The thorax is mostly for movement, holding legs and wings. The digestive organs are in the abdomen.

options.label: The exoskeleton
options.feedback: The exoskeleton is the outer covering, not a container for organs. The organs are inside the body, mainly in the abdomen.

items.ok_line: The abdomen holds the digestive organs.
items.ko_line: Digestive organs are in the abdomen, not the head or thorax.
items.exp_text: The abdomen is the large rear section of an insect. It holds most of the internal organs, including the stomach, intestines, and heart, and it is also where the insect's reproductive organs are found.

items.prompt: Which of these animals is an insect?

options.label: A grasshopper
options.feedback: Correct. A grasshopper has a head, thorax, abdomen, six legs, and two antennae, so it is an insect.

options.label: A spider
options.feedback: A spider has eight legs and no antennae, so it is not an insect. It is an arachnid.

options.label: A centipede
options.feedback: A centipede has many legs, sometimes over a hundred, and a long flat body. That is not an insect.

options.label: A crab
options.feedback: A crab has ten legs and lives in water. It is a crustacean, not an insect.

items.ok_line: A grasshopper is a true insect.
items.ko_line: Spiders, centipedes, and crabs are not insects.
items.exp_text: To be an insect, an animal must have three body sections, six legs, and two antennae. A grasshopper fits all of these, while spiders have eight legs and no antennae, so they belong to a different group.

items.prompt: What material is an insect's exoskeleton made of?

options.label: Bone
options.feedback: Bone is what vertebrates have inside their bodies. Insect exoskeletons are made of a different material called chitin.

options.label: Calcium and shell
options.feedback: Calcium carbonate makes snail shells and crab shells, not insect exoskeletons. Insects use chitin.

options.label: A tough substance called chitin
options.feedback: Correct. Chitin is a strong, flexible material that forms the hard outer layer of an insect's body.

options.label: Wax and oil
options.feedback: Wax may coat some insects to prevent drying, but it is not the main material of the exoskeleton. That is chitin.

items.ko_line: Insects use chitin, not bone or shell.
items.exp_text: An insect's exoskeleton is composed of chitin, a strong and somewhat flexible material. Chitin gives the body its hardness while still allowing movement at the joints.
